mcqs.question: Why does a downstream service sometimes start a disconnected, brand-new trace instead of continuing an existing one?
options: An outbound call failed to forward the trace context header (like `traceparent`), so the downstream service has no way to know it's part of an existing trace
The trace ID expires after exactly one service hop by design
Tracing backends only support traces spanning at most two services
The downstream service is running an incompatible programming language
mcqs.explanation: Trace continuity depends entirely on propagating the context header across each hop; if that header is dropped, the receiving service has no signal that it belongs to an existing trace and starts fresh. There's no built-in hop limit or language restriction involved.

mcqs.question: What's the key advantage of tail-based sampling over head-based sampling?
options: It requires no buffering infrastructure, unlike head-based sampling
It decides which traces to keep after seeing the full trace's outcome, so it can guarantee keeping every error or slow trace rather than risking discarding one before its outcome is known
It's always cheaper to run than head-based sampling
It only works for traces with a single span
mcqs.explanation: Tail-based sampling's advantage is precisely that it waits to see how a trace turned out before deciding, so interesting traces are never lost to an early, blind decision -- at the cost of buffering, which head-based sampling avoids by deciding upfront.

mcqs.question: Why is tracing 100% of requests in a high-traffic production service often a bad default?
options: 100% sampling makes context propagation stop working
Tracing at 100% is technically impossible regardless of traffic volume
The volume of span data can exceed what the tracing backend can affordably ingest or store, risking dropped spans or a backend outage
It's only a problem if the service has fewer than four downstream calls
mcqs.explanation: The issue is purely about ingest volume and cost at scale, not a technical impossibility or an effect on context propagation, which works the same regardless of sampling rate.

mcqs.question: A request's trace disappears the moment a producer publishes a message onto a queue for a consumer to pick up later. What's the most likely cause?
options: The tracing backend has a maximum trace lifetime shorter than the queue's delivery delay
The trace context wasn't written into the message's own attributes before publishing, so the consumer has nothing to extract and starts a new trace
Queues are fundamentally incompatible with any form of tracing
The consumer service is using a different tracing vendor
mcqs.explanation: Unlike an HTTP call, a queue hop has no live request carrying headers — the trace context must be explicitly injected into the message and extracted by the consumer. Missing that step breaks continuity; it isn't about backend lifetime limits, vendor mismatches, or an inherent incompatibility with queues.
